messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Tuan Nguyen was sixty-two when his grandson, Leo, took critically ill. The pediatric ward became a blur of fluorescent lights and the sharp, antiseptic scent of the ICU. He remembered the monitor’s frantic beeping, the attending physician’s urgent tone, and the crushing realization that he was merely a bystander to a process that could erase the boy in an instant. Leo survived, but the ordeal left Tuan with a fractured narrative that he could not piece together for himself. He would try to recount the days to the nurses, but the moments refused to settle into a linear sequence. Instead, the memories arrived unbidden, hyper-vivid and suffocatingly immediate, as if the sterile air were still pressing against his chest. Over the following months, this unspooling recollection bled into his daily life, leaving him certain that he had been irrevocably altered for the worse. He looked in the mirror and saw a stranger, a man whose core had been sanded down by fear. This profound sense of permanent damage made him certain that those around him were unreliable, their assurances of safety little more than polite façades. His distorted view of himself and others quickly dictated how he moved through the world. Because he believed he had permanently changed for the worse and could no longer trust the benevolent intentions of people, Tuan began to systematically withdraw from any situation that might demand vulnerability. When his daughter suggested he see a therapist, he flatly refused, steering the conversation toward household chores instead. He could not bear the idea of surrendering his inner turmoil to another person, fearing they would see through him. This deep-seated distrust of others became the engine of his daily conduct; he started avoiding medical clinics and hospitals altogether, convincing himself that staying behind locked doors was the only way to maintain control. The nature of his recollections further cemented these retreats. When the hospital memories surfaced, they did not arrive as distant reflections but as visceral, present-tense intrusions that made his hands tremble. The intensity of these moments was so overwhelming that he found himself scrambling to block them out, forcing his attention onto the television screen or the rhythmic folding of laundry to create a mental buffer. He pushed the recollections down with relentless force, telling himself that if he simply refused to engage with the past, it would lose its grip. This compulsive suppression and the constant need to occupy his mind became non-negotiable habits, dictating his schedule and isolating him from the community he needed to navigate. Yet, the more he fought the memories, the more his internal landscape hardened into certainty. The unrelenting vividness of the ICU moments convinced him that the world was fundamentally unpredictable and that any attempt to make sense of it was futile. Every time the trauma felt present, it reinforced the conviction that he had been permanently damaged, leaving him with a fractured sense of self that could never recover its former clarity. He began to interpret every minor slight as confirmation that people were not what they seemed. The memories did not just haunt him; they actively rewired his judgments, turning uncertainty into a blanket of suspicion that made him question the sincerity of every interaction. His own coping mechanisms, however, only fed the very cycles he feared. By refusing to process the trauma and instead stuffing his mind with distractions, Tuan ensured that the unspoken memories festered in his unconscious. The harder he tried to suppress the thoughts, the more they leaked through in fragmented, sensory bursts that bypassed his conscious control. His avoidance of medical care and psychological help meant that the original event remained frozen in time, never integrated, which in turn made the intrusions feel even more raw and unmanageable. The strategies meant to protect him actually acted as a magnifying glass, amplifying the vividness of the past and leaving him with no coherent story to anchor his present. Now at sixty-nine, Tuan works as a nanny for a family in a quiet suburban neighborhood, a role that inadvertently places him directly within the triggers he has spent decades avoiding. Every afternoon, as he changes diapers and prepares bottles, the sterile scent of baby wipes and the sharp cry of a fussy infant instantly pull him back to the ICU monitors. He manages the immediate panic by gripping his keys and focusing intently on the precise folding of the baby’s socks, forcing his mind to stay locked on the tactile task until his breathing evens out. The weight of his isolation has accumulated over years; his daughter visits less often, and he has stopped answering calls from former colleagues. What finally brought Tuan to the clinic was a Tuesday afternoon when a simple fever in the child in his care mirrored the crisis he once survived. The sight of the rapid pulse oximeter on the bassinet made him certain he could no longer rely on his own methods of suppression. He drove himself to the community health center, his hands shaking on the steering wheel, hoping against his ingrained distrust that a professional might finally help him untangle the story he cannot tell himself. He does not expect to feel better immediately; he only hopes that someone might finally give him a language for the unrecognizable man he has become, and perhaps allow him to step out from behind the locked doors he has built.
